molecular_identifier: PubChem CID 135398735; ChEMBL CHEMBL374478; CAS 13292-46-1; InChIKey JQXXHWHPUNPDRT-WLSIYKJHSA-N
mechanism_of_action: Inhibits bacterial DNA-dependent RNA polymerase by binding the beta subunit (RpoB), thereby blocking RNA synthesis
adme: Absorption: Readily absorbed orally; food can reduce absorption. Distribution: Widely distributed; approximately 80% protein bound. Metabolism: Hepatic deacetylation produces 25-desacetylrifampicin and enterohepatic circulation occurs. Excretion: Eliminated mainly through bile/feces, with a smaller proportion excreted in urine.
safety_toxicity: Documented adverse effects include hepatotoxicity, gastrointestinal reactions, hypersensitivity reactions, and hematologic adverse effects. Clinically apparent liver injury is well documented but uncommon.
known_limitations: Resistance can arise through mutations affecting the rifampicin target, particularly the RpoB/RNA-polymerase beta subunit.

molecular_identifier: PubChem CID 3767; ChEMBL CHEMBL64; CAS 54-85-3; InChIKey QRXWMOHMRWLFEY-UHFFFAOYSA-N
target: InhA (enoyl-ACP reductase) after activation by the mycobacterial KatG catalase-peroxidase
mechanism_of_action: Isoniazid is a prodrug activated by mycobacterial KatG; the activated species forms an NAD adduct that inhibits InhA and disrupts mycolic-acid synthesis.
potency: Minimal tuberculostatic concentration reported as 0.025–0.05 µg/mL; experimental context should be considered before comparison with other potency measurements.
selectivity: High antimicrobial specificity toward susceptible mycobacteria is reported; a quantitative cross-target selectivity profile was not established in this extraction.
adme: Absorption: rapidly and almost completely absorbed orally; food can reduce absorption. Distribution: diffuses widely into body fluids and cells, including cerebrospinal fluid. Metabolism: primarily hepatic acetylation involving NAT2, with acetylator phenotype affecting disposition. Excretion: predominantly renal, with most of a dose excreted in urine as unchanged drug and metabolites.
safety_toxicity: Important safety concerns include hepatotoxicity and peripheral neuropathy; other adverse reactions and drug interactions are documented in pharmacological and regulatory sources.
known_limitations: Resistance can arise through mutations affecting the drug-activation pathway or target; variability in NAT2 acetylation also contributes to differences in disposition.
missing_information: Detailed quantitative selectivity profile; additional assay-specific potency measurements

target: Multiple reported molecular targets/pathways; PanD (aspartate decarboxylase) and RpsA (ribosomal protein S1) have been implicated, while PncA is responsible for activation of the prodrug
mechanism_of_action: Pyrazinamide is converted by the mycobacterial PncA pyrazinamidase to pyrazinoic acid (POA). POA has been reported to disrupt membrane energetics and transport and to affect pathways including coenzyme A biosynthesis and trans-translation. The exact overall mechanism remains complex.
selectivity: A quantitative cross-target selectivity profile was not established in this extraction.
adme: Absorption: rapidly absorbed after oral administration. Distribution: widely distributed into body tissues and fluids. Metabolism: converted to pyrazinoic acid and further metabolized. Excretion: predominantly renal, with metabolites and unchanged drug eliminated in urine.
safety_toxicity: Important safety evidence includes hepatotoxicity and elevations of serum aminotransferases; other adverse effects are documented in pharmacological and regulatory sources.
known_limitations: The mechanism of action is complex and has historically been incompletely resolved. Resistance is strongly associated with mutations in pncA, while mutations affecting other pathways including rpsA and panD have also been reported.
missing_information: Quantitative potency; quantitative selectivity; detailed assay-specific evidence

mechanism_of_action: Inhibits mycobacterial arabinosyltransferases involved in arabinan biosynthesis, disrupting mycobacterial cell-wall formation
adme: Absorption: well absorbed orally. Distribution: widely distributed and penetrates several tissues and body fluids. Metabolism: limited metabolism. Excretion: predominantly renal, with substantial unchanged drug eliminated in urine.
safety_toxicity: Important safety concern is optic toxicity, including visual-acuity and color-vision disturbances; renal impairment can increase exposure.
known_limitations: Optic toxicity limits the safety profile; resistance can occur through changes involving embCAB and related pathways.
missing_information: Quantitative potency; quantitative selectivity; detailed assay-specific evidence

safety_toxicity: Important safety considerations include QT-interval prolongation and hepatotoxicity; regulatory safety monitoring is required.
supporting_publications: WHO TB research and innovation; PubChem CID 5388906

safety_toxicity: QT-interval prolongation is an important safety consideration; gastrointestinal and other adverse effects are documented.
supporting_publications: WHO TB research and innovation; PubChem
known_limitations: Resistance may involve alterations in the nitroreductase/F420 activation pathway; QT prolongation is an important limitation.
